name: Flexitarian diet

lead: The flexitarian diet centres on plants, such as vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains, while allowing meat and other animal foods in smaller amounts or on some days. It is a flexible middle path between omnivorous and vegetarian eating.

For appearance, people use it as a way to manage weight and body fat with a higher-fibre, lower-calorie pattern while keeping enough protein to train. Reviews describe observational links between reduced red meat and lower diabetes and heart-disease risk; the definition of "flexitarian" varies a lot across studies.

paras: Practitioners build meals around plant foods and add smaller portions of meat, fish, eggs or dairy on chosen days, with meat-free days or weeks being a common structure. Athletes and lifters adapting it focus on plant protein sources and meeting protein needs.

Well-planned versions can meet nutrition recommendations, while poorly planned ones may cause deficiencies, reviewers say. Researchers have also discussed whether restrictive eating motives overlap with weight-control behaviours in some people.

chain: More vegetables, legumes and whole grains
Higher fibre and lower calorie density with adequate protein
Easier weight control and a leaner look
angle.text: People use flexitarian eating to keep body fat down while still getting protein from some animal sources and plant proteins. Athletes use plant-forward patterns while meeting protein needs.

lead: The flexitarian diet, also called semi-vegetarian, is a plant-centred eating pattern that allows limited meat and other animal products. Definitions vary by country and study; a Dutch group, for example, counts anyone who skips meat, fish and cold cuts for at least one day a week.[1]

People adopt it for weight management, general health and, in some cases, a leaner physique and better-looking skin through diet quality. Research summaries link reduced red-meat intake with lower risks of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, though much of this is observational.[1][2] A 2018 review asked whether flexitarian eating helps weight control or can mask restrictive eating.[3]
infobox: Merriam-Webster 2012; American Dialect Society word of the year 2003 [1]

paras: The pattern emphasises fruit, vegetables, legumes and whole grains and reduces meat rather than eliminating it; related terms include demi-vegetarianism, reducetarianism and semi-veganism.[1] Wikipedia reports that the word gained wide use in the 2010s, entered Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary in 2012 and was voted most useful word of 2003 by the American Dialect Society.[1]

Self-identification is common and loose: in the Netherlands, flexitarian identification rose from 14% in 2011 to 43% in 2019 while those people reported eating meat on more days per week, leading researchers to suspect the label had grown elastic.[1]

A 2016 review in Frontiers in Nutrition surveyed the evidence on flexitarian diets and health.[2] A review of plant-based diet definitions describes where flexitarian patterns sit among vegetarian and vegan diets.[4][5]

For physique goals, a review of sustainable diets for athletes names meeting, not exceeding, protein requirements through flexitarian and plant-based approaches as one option, and calls for more research on training adaptation.[6] A randomized trial in healthy adults examined replacing animal with plant proteins for 12 weeks and found changes in vitamin and mineral intake and status.[7]
Reviewers also note that plant-based meat alternatives differ nutritionally from traditional plant foods.[8]

A 10-week trial compared a flexitarian diet including red meat with a vegetarian diet including plant-based meat alternatives and examined adherence and eating experiences.[9] Prescribing vegetarian or flexitarian diets has been reported to lead to a sustained reduction in meat intake.[10]
The 2018 review notes that balanced low-meat diets tend to be lower in calories and that weight control is a motive for some people, while cautioning against over-generalizing to all vegetarians.[3]

Controlled trials exist on plant-protein substitution and adherence: a 12-week randomized trial of replacing animal proteins with plant proteins,[7] a 10-week randomized flexitarian-versus-vegetarian trial,[9] and randomized crossover studies of plant protein and metabolic markers.[11] Wikipedia notes that most flexitarian evidence is observational, and that environmental benefits come largely from modelling.[1]
